articles.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Melania Trump claims to have secured ceasefire for single Ukrainian town - inkl
articles.summary: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Melania Trump claims to have secured ceasefire for single Ukrainian town  inkl
articles.full_text:
The White House has praised Melania Trump for reportedly securing a ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where up to 2,000 residents are cut off from world and facing starvation.
Russia has agreed to pause all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway, according to the White House.

articles.title: Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and China coordinating logistics along Middle Corridor - Eurasianet
articles.summary: Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and China coordinating logistics along Middle Corridor  Eurasianet
articles.full_text:
BACKGROUND:
On September 9, 2026, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s interview with Xinhua highlighted the growing importance of the Azerbaijan–Kazakhstan-China logistics connection. The same day in Baku, at the CICA Conference of Port Authorities, Jiang Wei, Vice President for External Relations of Lianyungang Port, proposed incorporating Baku into the existing Lianyungang–Khorgos–Aktau “Three Nodes” logistics chain.
On the sidelines of the conference, Rovshan Rustamov, Chairman of Azerbaijan Railways (ADY), met with representatives of China’s Shanghai International Port Group (SIPG), NIZE Tech, and LianyungangPort. Discussions focused on developing the Lianyungang–Baku route, expanding regular container and block-train services, attracting additional Chinese cargo bound for Europe, and introducing smart-port technologies and digital solutions. Participants also highlighted the importance of exchanging information on cargo forecasts, train schedules, and logistical requirements to improve coordination between railway and port operations and strengthen the Middle Corridor’s competitiveness.
On September 8, Tahir Budagov, Deputy Chairman of Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), met with a Chinese delegation led by Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee. Their discussions focused on trade, transportation, the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), a trans-Armenia corridor and Beijing’s support for Azerbaijan’s deeper engagement with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
These developments build on a growing network of infrastructure investments and bilateral agreements established in previous years, supported by sustained high-level engagement among the participating governments. On July 3, 2024, Azerbaijan and China adopted a Joint Declaration on the Establishment of a Strategic Partnership in Astana. The declaration committed both countries to strengthening cooperation on the Middle Corridor and accelerating the development of China–Europe freight-train services. That same day, KTZ Express, AktauInternational CommercialSea Port, and Lianyungang Port Group reached an agreement on the key terms for establishing a joint venture to develop a container hub at Aktau Port. The US$ 96 million project envisaged the construction, management, and operation of a new container terminal with a planned annual capacity of 500,000 TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent unit).
In September 2024, Lianyungang Port Group Co., Ltd., Kazakhstan Express Rail Company, and AktauInternational CommercialSea Port signed agreements to implement the Aktau Port Container Hub project. The facility officially began operations on June 9, 2025, strengthening Kazakhstan’s transit capacity along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. Meanwhile, in November 2024, during COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and China’s Xi’an Free Trade Port Construction and Operation Co., Ltd. agreed to establish a joint venture to develop an intermodal cargo terminal on an initial 40-hectare site at the Port of Baku in Alat. In April 2025, the transport ministers of Azerbaijan and China inked the Agreement on International Multimodal Transportation in Beijing. In July 2025, Azerbaijan Railways (ADY) concluded separate agreements with China State Railway Group and Xi’an Free Trade Port to strengthen the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway, expand rail transit, and establish a container yard at Xi’an with an annual handling capacity of 20,000 TEUs.
These joint initiatives establish the foundations for a logistics network connecting Chinese inland and coastal transport hubs with Kazakhstan’s railways and Caspian ports, Azerbaijan’s transport infrastructure, and onward routes to Europe.
IMPLICATIONS:
The proposed extension of the Lianyungang–Khorgos–Aktau chain to Baku represents a shift from developing individual transport projects toward coordinating a broader logistics network. The initiative seeks to connect existing facilities through more integrated freight services and information systems.
Azerbaijan’s greater integration into the trans-Eurasian maritime network could strengthen China’s connectivity with markets west of the Caspian Sea and improve links between its inland logistics centers and European destinations. With an annual cargo throughput of 367 million tons and 7.1598 million TEUs, Lianyungang Port serves as a key transit gateway connecting China’s maritime trade routes with its inland transport networks, while Khorgos facilitates cross-border rail connectivity between China and the wider Caspian–Central Asia region. Aktau provides access to the Caspian Sea, while Baku serves as a gateway to the South Caucasus and onward transport routes through Georgia and Türkiye. With a planned annual cargo-handling capacity of 25 million tons, the Port of Baku is positioned to play a vital role in strengthening Eurasian connectivity. Closer integration with the Lianyungang–Khorgos–Aktau network could reinforce Azerbaijan’s strategic importance in the trans-Caspian trade and logistics ecosystem.
Closer coordination with Baku is also enabling Astana to better leverage its Caspian logistics infrastructure and reinforce its position along westbound trade routes. To expand the Middle Corridor’s capacity, Kazakhstan plans to increase the combined cargo-handling capacity of the Aktau and Kuryk ports from 21 million to 30 million tons through modernization efforts. Authorities in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have been working to improve trans-Caspian freight transport along the Baku–Aktau route. As part of these efforts, an electronic data exchange system was introduced between the two ports in April 2025 to enhance inter-port coordination, streamline cargo operations, and improve freight efficiency across the Caspian basin.
Moreover, given the proximity of LianyungangPort to major maritime hubs in Japan and South Korea, the Lianyungang–Khorgos–Aktau–Baku logistics chain could provide both countries with an additional trade route into the wider Caspian-Central Asian region. Amid escalating geopolitical tensions, sanctions-related constraints, and disruptions linked to the war in Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Persian Gulf, the Middle Corridor is gaining prominence as a potentially more resilient supply channel for both countries. Tokyo and Seoul have already expanded their engagement with Central Asia through multilateral cooperation frameworks that strongly support their involvement in the Middle Corridor’s development.
Despite the expansion of transport infrastructure, integrating the Lianyungang–Khorgos–Aktau–Baku route into a commercially competitive logistics network will require overcoming several operational challenges. Differences in railway timetables, port-handling procedures, customs documentation, and cargo-tracking systems can cause delays at transfer points, particularly where shipments move between rail and maritime transport. Limited digitalization of transport and customs procedures, together with the lack of interoperable information systems and real-time data sharing among participating countries, could further hinder cargo tracking, information exchange, and coordination among logistics operators.
Caspian crossings add another layer of complexity, as vessel availability, weather conditions, and the coordination of loading and unloading operations can affect transit schedules. The Caspian Sea’s declining water levels pose an additional long-term challenge by potentially reducing navigable depths, restricting vessel access to ports, and increasing dredging requirements and transportation costs. These conditions could further disrupt maritime operations and undermine the reliability of transit schedules along the Middle Corridor. Ostensibly, infrastructure expansion alone will not guarantee higher freight volumes if tariffs remain uncompetitive or cargo owners cannot rely on predictable delivery times.
Addressing these constraints will require closer coordination among railway operators, port authorities, customs administrations, and logistics companies, supported by interoperable digital systems and reliable information-sharing mechanisms. Efficient transshipment operations, adequate vessel capacity, streamlined customs procedures, and dependable rail connections will be essential to reducing logistical uncertainty and facilitating the movement of intercontinental cargo across the Caspian Sea.
CONCLUSIONS:
The developments outlined above indicate that Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and China are moving toward closer coordination in developing the Middle Corridor’s logistics network. The proposed integration of Baku into Lianyungang’s “Three Nodes” logistics chain builds on container-handling infrastructure at Aktau, plans for an intermodal terminal at the Port of Baku, and agreements connecting Chinese logistics hubs with Azerbaijan’s railway network. The key challenge lies in transforming these individual projects into reliable, integrated freight services. Progress in these areas could further consolidate Azerbaijan’s role as a regional transit hub, strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in Caspian connectivity, and expand China’s access to markets across the wider Caspian–Central Asian region and beyond.
This article was originally published by the Central Asia-Caucasus Analyst and reprinted under a partner post arrangement with Eurasianet.
Vusal Guliyev is an Indo-Pacific and Eurasian Affairs Analyst with professional and academic experience spanning leading research institutions, think tanks, and fellowship programs across Azerbaijan, Türkiye, China, Japan, South Korea, and the United States. He currently works as a Leading Advisor at the Baku-based Center for Analysis of International Relations and Multiculturalism (AIR Center).

articles.title: Zheenbek Kulubaev took part in the first meeting of the foreign ministers of Central Asian countries and Georgia - open.kg
articles.summary: Zheenbek Kulubaev took part in the first meeting of the foreign ministers of Central Asian countries and Georgia  open.kg
articles.full_text:
The first meeting of the foreign ministers of Central Asia and Georgia took place in Batumi, with the participation of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan, Jeenbek Kulubaev. This event was initiated by the Georgian side and marked an important step in strengthening regional cooperation.
During two sessions dedicated to political dialogue and regional interaction, participants discussed ways to strengthen political ties and expand trade and economic cooperation. Topics such as transport logistics, energy, tourism, and humanitarian contacts were also considered, highlighting a multilateral approach to developing relations.
Kulubaev emphasized the importance of this format of meetings for aligning approaches to pressing issues at both regional and international levels. He pointed out that deepening relations between Central Asia and Georgia could contribute to the development of connections between Asia and Europe, opening new horizons for cooperation.
The Kyrgyz delegation underscored the necessity of developing political dialogue and practical interaction in key sectors. Joint efforts were proposed for diversifying trade routes, digital transformation, attracting investments, and developing industrial cooperation, which will contribute to the economic growth of the regions.

articles.title: Uzbekistan, Polish firms explore joint manufacturing, export projects - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Polish firms explore joint manufacturing, export projects  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. A delegation of entrepreneurs from Uzbekistan’s Tashkent region is exploring investment and trade opportunities in Poland, focusing on agriculture, water management, industrial manufacturing and medicinal plant processing, the regional administration said on October 23.
The delegation, led by Dilshod Rasulov, head of the Tashkent region project office of Uzbekistan’s Agency for Industrial Cooperation and Public Procurement, is meeting with Polish government officials, industry organizations and major manufacturers to expand bilateral economic ties and develop joint projects.
The first round of talks involved Jacek Czerniak, Poland’s deputy minister of agriculture, and Piotr Kolada, head of the National Support Centre for Agriculture (KOWR). The discussions focused on increasing bilateral trade, diversifying exports and addressing transport and logistics challenges.
The sides also highlighted the potential of the Polish-Uzbek Trade House, established in Ohangaron district of Tashkent region, to strengthen commercial ties and help businesses from both countries expand their market presence.
The delegation also met with Jacek Jarząbek, vice president of Wody Polskie, and representatives of Poland’s Ministry of Infrastructure. The talks covered water resource management, reservoir operations, water storage systems and improvements to canals and pumping stations. The sides also explored the use of drones and artificial intelligence to digitize water management and improve operational efficiency.
Plans were outlined to organize an online meeting between representatives of Uzbekistan’s Uzsuvtaminot water utility and Polish specialists, as well as to strengthen cooperation between the relevant government agencies.
As part of the visit, the delegation examined operations at Polish manufacturers, including Pronar, which produces agricultural and municipal machinery. The parties explored potential equipment supplies, manufacturing cooperation and joint projects.
At Dary Natury, a Polish company specializing in organic food products and medicinal plants, the delegation examined processing and packaging operations. The sides also considered opportunities to export medicinal plants grown in Uzbekistan to Poland for processing and subsequent sale as finished products.

articles.title: Turkmenistan, Georgia discuss expanding trade, transport cooperation - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Turkmenistan, Georgia discuss expanding trade, transport cooperation  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Turkmenistan and Georgia have discussed expanding cooperation in trade, transport and logistics, with a focus on improving connectivity and making fuller use of existing transit corridors.
According to a statement published by Turkmenistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the talks took place in Batumi on October 22 between Rashid Meredov, Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkmenistan, and Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.
The ministers reviewed bilateral relations in the political, diplomatic, trade and economic, transport and logistics, and humanitarian spheres, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening cooperation.
Particular attention was given to expanding transit opportunities and making more effective use of existing transport corridors linking the two countries. The sides also discussed cooperation within the United Nations and other international organizations.
The meeting followed Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s state visit to Georgia in July 2026, during which the two countries signed several documents aimed at strengthening cooperation in railway and maritime transport.
These included a memorandum of understanding between Turkmenistan’s Ministry of Railway Transport and Georgian Railway JSC to deepen cooperation in the railway sector.
Additional agreements involving Turkmenistan’s State Service of Maritime and River Transport and Georgian organizations focused on maritime transport safety, specialist training and maritime education.

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia Trade Deadly Strikes After U.S. Tries to Reboot Peace Talks - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia Trade Deadly Strikes After U.S. Tries to Reboot Peace Talks  The Moscow Times
articles.full_text:
Ukraine and Russia exchanged a flurry of drone and missile attacks overnight, leaving at least seven dead across Ukraine and one person killed in southwestern Russia, officials in the two warring countries said Thursday morning.
Authorities in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine said a man was killed when a Ukrainian drone crashed into the truck he was driving. In a separate strike in the region, a man riding a motorcycle was wounded.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 Ukrainian drones had been tracked in the skies above the wider Moscow region overnight, with air defense systems intercepting 163 of the unmanned aircraft that were on a direct approach to the city. Two people were wounded in the Voronovo district, located to the southwest of central Moscow.
There were also reports of an explosion and fire south of the capital. The exiled news outlet Astra, using eyewitness footage of the fire, identified the targeted facility as a storage and logistics facility belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate, located in Serpukhov.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify those reports.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 808 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
Russian officials reported injuries in the border regions of Kursk amid the overnight air barrage. Residential buildings in the Lipetsk region were also damaged. Power lines were knocked down in the Voronezh and Kaluga regions.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed at least seven people across the country, including three in Zaporizhzhia, two in Donetsk, one in Sumy and a woman in the Kharkiv region.
The exchange of attacks came just hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff concluded talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss renewing trilateral peace negotiations that have stalled since February.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that Kyiv supported a U.S. proposal for three-way talks with Moscow and Washington. The Kremlin said Putin had agreed to resume the U.S.-mediated talks as early as next month.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title: India, Azerbaijan seek stronger trade and energy ties in Baku - India Today
articles.summary: India, Azerbaijan seek stronger trade and energy ties in Baku  India Today
articles.full_text:
S Jaishankar and Jeyhun Bayramov held talks in Baku to expand bilateral cooperation. The meeting signalled closer coordination on commerce, connectivity, energy and regional diplomacy.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar held talks with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov on Friday, focusing on strengthening cooperation in trade, investment, energy, tourism and connectivity, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
During his day-long visit to Azerbaijan, Jaishankar also discussed regional and international developments, cooperation in multilateral forums and ways to deepen political and people-to-people ties between the two countries.
In a press statement after the meeting in Baku, Jaishankar described the discussions as “very productive” and said they had helped chart the way forward for bilateral relations. “Our talks dwelt on further expanding our bilateral relations. We spoke about economic cooperation, including in trade, investment and energy, which are central to our bilateral ties. Given our complementary economies, we believe that there is very good scope for further enhancement of our bilateral trade and investment,” he said.
The two ministers also discussed ongoing activities and exchanges and ways to take them forward. On connectivity, Jaishankar said both countries were involved in the International North-South Transport Corridor and had agreed to coordinate more closely.
“We spoke about connectivity, because that is so important in a globalised economy. We are both invested in the International North-South Transport Corridor. That's very important for us. We agreed today that we will coordinate more closely in that regard,” he said.
The 7,200-km corridor is a transport network designed to move freight among India, Iran, Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, Central Asia and Europe. India supports the project.
In a post on X, Jaishankar said the two sides had agreed to deepen political consultations, increase visits, expand economic activity, improve connectivity and promote people-to-people ties. He also said they had agreed to strengthen cooperation in oil and energy and extend it to other sectors.
Bayramov said he was delighted to welcome Jaishankar and exchange views on the state and prospects of Azerbaijan-India relations, including political dialogue, trade and investment, energy, tourism and cultural ties. “We also discussed regional and international developments, and cooperation within multilateral frameworks. Emphasised the importance of continued dialogue and exploring opportunities for cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” he posted on X.
On air connectivity, Jaishankar said daily flights were operating but both sides needed to consider ways to increase them further. He also thanked Bayramov for helping evacuate Indian nationals, particularly students, from Iran during the conflict earlier this year. “We have Indian students in Azerbaijan. I want to thank you for the care and consideration with which you look after them,” PTI quoted him as saying.
Jaishankar suggested resuming and increasing the participation of Azerbaijani professionals from different fields in the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation programme.
Referring to regional developments, Jaishankar welcomed the August peace agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia and expressed hope that it would lead to lasting peace. “India has a very clear position that disputes should be settled through dialogue and diplomacy. And in that context, we had, of course, our discussions covered the Middle East, Europe and Eurasia,” he said.
He said the two sides had assessed the global impact of conflicts, particularly on economies in the Global South, which faced problems related to food, fuel, fertiliser and finance. “We have a common interest in really promoting peace and progress and prosperity,” he said, adding that terrorism, conflict and instability were “our common enemies”.
Jaishankar said the two countries had also exchanged views on reforming and expanding international and regional organisations to make them more contemporary and relevant. He invited Bayramov to visit India at a convenient time.
Earlier, Jaishankar called on Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties. He conveyed greetings from President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Jaishankar said his visit followed the recent meeting between Modi and Aliyev on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
“Our discussions were focused; they were forward-looking, and we exchanged views on various aspects of our relationship. In fact, the President was kind enough to give a lot of time to review really the entire gamut of our ties, including ongoing cooperation, what we could be doing more, what we could be doing differently,” Jaishankar said.
“We also discussed important regional and global developments from a strategic perspective,” he said, adding that both countries were independently minded and could take their own positions on important issues.
The two sides agreed to exchange trade delegations and groups working in other areas of cooperation. Jaishankar said India and Azerbaijan shared a long history of cultural and people-to-people exchanges. “We respect each other's culture and values, and that provides a very good foundation to work towards a more contemporary partnership,” he said.
He said mechanisms such as Foreign Office Consultations could provide a detailed roadmap for developing bilateral ties. Referring to a recent visit by the Minister of State for External Affairs to Baku for the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, Jaishankar said India highly valued Azerbaijan's chairmanship of the grouping.
The visit focused on expanding India-Azerbaijan relations through stronger economic cooperation, better connectivity, greater exchanges and continued dialogue on regional and global issues.

articles.title: Opinion: China’s Regional Strategy Meets Central Asia’s National Bargains - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Opinion: China’s Regional Strategy Meets Central Asia’s National Bargains  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway spent decades on the drawing board. Disagreements over its route and financing held it up long after the three governments endorsed the project. In 2024, a Kyrgyz parliamentarian asked railway officials a simple question: “Where will we find $1 billion?”
A financing agreement signed in Bishkek on December 16, 2025, cleared a major obstacle. The railway is estimated to cost $4.7 billion. Chinese banks will lend about $2.3 billion to the joint project company over 35 years. China holds 51% of the company, while Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan each hold 24.5%. The partners will provide the remaining funding as equity.
In June 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s parliament approved in the first reading a separate $304.5 million loan from China’s Export-Import Bank to help fund its own contribution. That loan has a 25-year term. The joint company’s debt and Kyrgyzstan’s borrowing for its stake are different obligations, but both affect how much value the country will need to earn from the line.
Kyrgyzstan wants business around the railway, including terminals and freight services; Uzbekistan gains a direct rail link toward China, while Beijing gains another route west. The governments agreed to build the line, but tariffs and terminal operations will help decide how the returns are shared.
The same division between shared goals and separate deals runs through China’s C+C5 relationship with the five Central Asian states.
At the second China-Central Asia summit in Astana in June 2025, the six countries signed a treaty on eternal good-neighborliness. The Chinese Foreign Ministry also published a list of 55 cooperation documents. The first 14 cover the regional China-Central Asia framework. The other 41 involve Chinese institutions and counterparts in individual Central Asian countries, including local authorities and companies.
The count reflects how the agreements are organized rather than their financial weight. The regional documents cover road permits, customs procedures and green minerals. The country-specific agreements extend into particular industries and investment relationships.
Customs cooperation shows how regional talks can lead to bilateral action. At a meeting on May 21–22, 2025, customs chiefs from China and Central Asia agreed to joint border inspections. The next day, Chinese and Kazakh officials conducted an inspection of Nur Zholy-Khorgos. They agreed to accept more trucks from Kazakhstan and recognize each other’s X-ray inspection images to reduce repeat checks.
Kazakhstan’s customs authority explicitly linked the inspection to the regional meeting. The agreement illustrates how governments can address a shared concern through negotiations at an individual crossing.
The Astana investment agreements reflected different national priorities. Kazakhstan pursued investment protection and applications for China’s BeiDou satellite navigation system, while Kyrgyzstan signed documents on an AI application center and processing industries. These were country-specific arrangements within the wider regional framework.
The railway illustrates why some projects require only a few governments to agree. After recurring disagreements over its route and funding, China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan reached a financing settlement in 2025. They did not need all five Central Asian governments to negotiate a single position. Kazakhstan already has direct rail links with China; Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan stand to gain a new one. Their interests in future cargo flows may overlap without being identical.
Trade gives those choices greater weight. China’s Ministry of Commerce reported bilateral trade with Central Asia of $106.3 billion in 2025, up 12% on the previous year. China sold $71.2 billion in goods to the region and purchased $35.1 billion. Those totals conceal different trade patterns in each country. They also give governments a reason to seek more production and processing at home.
The Astana summit produced a regional memorandum on green-minerals investment. Actual mines and processing plants will still need contracts specifying who finances them and where the processing takes place. Customs technology raises a similar question. Shared electronic permits can speed freight, but countries must agree which systems can exchange data and who can access it.
Central Asian leaders already consult among themselves before many meetings with outside powers. Their own regional process has developed alongside the expanding C5+ diplomatic formats. Cooperation with China gives them further reason to coordinate where their commercial interests overlap.
The public record offers evidence of joint procedures and some action after regional meetings. It offers less detail on cases where all five governments secured shared financing conditions or common requirements for Chinese investment. Private negotiations may go further than the documents reveal.
Closer coordination need not mean adopting a single commercial policy. Governments could compare financing risks before committing to cross-border projects, giving each a fuller basis for negotiating its own terms.
The railway contracts and the Khorgos agreement show how China’s regional agenda takes shape through individual negotiations. For the countries hosting new connections, the terms will determine how much control they retain and how much income remains after the costs are paid.

articles.title: Eldor Aripov: China maintains position as leading trading partner for all five Central Asian countries - Dunyo
articles.summary: Eldor Aripov: China maintains position as leading trading partner for all five Central Asian countries  Dunyo
articles.full_text:
Eldor Aripov: China maintains position as leading trading partner for all five Central Asian countries
October 23, 2026. 16:00 • 3 min
• 311
BISHKEK, October 23. /Dunyo IA/. The sixth “China–Central Asia” Think Tank Forum, themed “High-Quality Development and Joint Modernization”, was held in Bishkek yesterday, reports Dunyo IA correspondent.
Forum brought together representatives of leading think tanks, government institutions and expert communities from China and the Central Asian countries to discuss prospects for regional cooperation and practical approaches to joint modernization.
Eldor Aripov, Director of the Institute for Strategic and Regional Studies under the President of Uzbekistan (ISRS), addressed the forum participants via video message. He outlined the key achievements and current priorities of cooperation between China and the Central Asian countries, placing particular emphasis on prospects for further strengthening the partnership.
ISRS Director highlighted the forum’s growing role in advancing regional cooperation. He noted that its inclusion in the outcome documents of two “China–Central Asia” summits demonstrated that the leaders of the participating countries view expert dialogue as an effective instrument of cooperation rather than a mere protocol formality.
Eldor Aripov emphasized that the Astana Declaration and the Treaty on Eternal Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation had laid a solid political foundation for the partnership, setting the course for cooperation over the coming decades.
Turning to trade and economic relations, the ISRS Director noted that in 2025, trade between China and the Central Asian countries exceeded $106 billion for the first time, marking a 12% year-on-year increase. China remains the leading trading partner of all five countries in the region.
Uzbekistan–China cooperation is also expanding steadily. Over the past five years, bilateral trade has tripled to nearly $18 billion, while Chinese investment has increased fivefold to $17 billion.
At the same time, Eldor Aripov stressed that the results achieved so far did not mean that all the objectives had been fulfilled. The current structure of trade, he noted, does not yet fully reflect the interests and potential of the partners.
Against this background, the development of transport networks is particularly important, including the construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. ISRS Director emphasized that new routes should do more than facilitate transit; they should evolve into fully fledged economic corridors.
He also highlighted the importance of deepening industrial and digital cooperation. This requires, above all, aligning standards, approaches to implementing joint projects and security protocols to establish sustainable economic ties between China and the countries of Central Asia.
Current phase of the partnership should be defined by a shift from expanding volumes to improving quality, from trade in goods to industrial cooperation, and from exchanging projects to sharing management experience.
ISRS Director stressed that modernization is effective only when partners learn from one another rather than simply replicate external models. This places greater responsibility on think tanks, which are expected to compare approaches, identify potential risks at an early stage and propose solutions before the need for them arises.
In this context, Eldor Aripov recalled that President of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev has repeatedly emphasized the important role of the expert community in long-term planning.
Concluding his address, Eldor Aripov expressed confidence that substantive and open dialogue would generate new ideas that could subsequently be translated into concrete policy decisions and give fresh impetus to cooperation between China and the Central Asian countries.

articles.title: Kazakhstan and China Launch Cross-Border Autonomous Freight Pilot - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Kazakhstan and China Launch Cross-Border Autonomous Freight Pilot  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan and China are advancing a landmark initiative to modernize Eurasian logistics, announcing a pilot project for autonomous freight transportation along their shared international border. The agreement, formalized between the Kazakh Road Research Institute (KazdorNII) and China TransInfo Group, establishes a joint competence center dedicated to developing and deploying driverless cargo technologies across one of the world's most critical overland trade corridors.
Automating the Middle Corridor
The pilot project targets the integration of autonomous heavy-duty trucks into the regular freight rotation between China and Kazakhstan. As global supply chains continue to seek alternatives to maritime routes disrupted by geopolitical friction, the overland Middle Corridor has seen a massive surge in cargo volumes. However, this growth has exposed significant logistical bottlenecks, including driver shortages, border crossing delays, and the high costs of long-haul human labor.
By introducing autonomous freight capabilities, Astana and Beijing aim to create a seamless, high-capacity logistics pipeline. Driverless trucks can operate around the clock without the physiological constraints of human drivers, potentially slashing transit times and reducing the operational costs of moving goods from Chinese manufacturing hubs to Central Asian distribution centers and onward to European markets. The initiative represents a strategic pivot toward technology-driven infrastructure, positioning the China-Kazakhstan border as a testing ground for next-generation supply chain automation.
Technology Transfer and Joint Competence
The core of the new partnership is the establishment of a Joint Competence Center, which will serve as the operational and intellectual hub for the autonomous freight rollout. China TransInfo Group, a leader in intelligent transport systems and smart city infrastructure, will provide the proprietary software, sensor arrays, and AI-driven navigation systems required for autonomous heavy vehicles.
In return, KazdorNII brings indispensable local expertise to the collaboration. The Kazakh institute will be responsible for adapting these advanced technologies to the specific environmental and infrastructural realities of Central Asia. This includes mapping road networks for autonomous navigation, establishing the necessary regulatory frameworks for driverless cross-border transit, and standardizing safety protocols. The technology transfer aspect of the agreement is particularly significant for Kazakhstan, as it seeks to build domestic capacity in artificial intelligence and automated logistics rather than merely acting as a passive consumer of foreign technology.
Building on Eurasian Precedents
This initiative does not exist in a vacuum; it builds upon a growing regional momentum toward unmanned cargo transport. Earlier in 2026, Kazakhstan successfully completed a cross-border autonomous freight pilot with Russia, demonstrating the viability of driverless trucks navigating the vast, sparsely populated steppes of the Eurasian Economic Union. That project provided crucial data on how autonomous systems perform in extreme weather conditions and across lengthy, unmonitored highway stretches.
The China-Kazakhstan corridor, however, presents a far more complex operational environment. The border crossings at Khorgos and Alashanku are among the busiest in the world, characterized by dense traffic, complex customs procedures, and mixed flows of automated and human-driven vehicles. Successfully deploying autonomous trucks in this environment will require advanced vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication systems and highly sophisticated edge computing capabilities to navigate the chaotic dynamics of international border logistics.
Logistical Bottlenecks and Regulatory Hurdles
Despite the technological promise, the path to full-scale commercial deployment is fraught with regulatory and infrastructural hurdles. Cross-border autonomous transport requires harmonization between two distinct legal jurisdictions. Chinese and Kazakh authorities must agree on liability frameworks in the event of an accident, data sharing protocols regarding cargo manifests, and unified standards for vehicle certification.
Furthermore, the physical infrastructure of the border zones must be upgraded to support autonomous navigation. This includes the installation of smart road sensors, dedicated 5G communication corridors, and automated customs clearance gantries that can interface directly with a driverless truck's onboard systems. If KazdorNII and China TransInfo can successfully navigate these complexities, the pilot project will not only transform bilateral trade but also establish a new blueprint for automated, transcontinental freight networks across the broader Belt and Road Initiative.
Geopolitical and Economic Integration
The deployment of autonomous freight corridors extends far beyond mere logistical efficiency; it is a profound exercise in geopolitical and economic integration. For China, securing a reliable, high-speed overland route through Kazakhstan is a vital component of the Belt and Road Initiative, ensuring that its exports can reach European markets without relying exclusively on vulnerable maritime chokepoints.
For Kazakhstan, the partnership accelerates its transition from a traditional transit state into a sophisticated logistics hub. By embedding Chinese AI and automation technologies into its national infrastructure, Astana deepens its economic interoperability with Beijing. This technological alignment creates long-term structural dependencies, ensuring that the Sino-Kazakh border remains a highly efficient, frictionless conduit for trade. As the pilot project moves from the planning phase to active road testing, it will serve as a critical barometer for the future of automated global commerce, demonstrating whether artificial intelligence can successfully bridge the physical and regulatory divides of international trade.

articles.title: Kazakhstan, Germany discuss industrial cooperation, transport corridors - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Kazakhstan, Germany discuss industrial cooperation, transport corridors  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Kazakhstan and Germany have discussed prospects for expanding industrial cooperation, attracting investment and developing international transport corridors, according to the Ministry of National Economy of Kazakhstan.
The issues were discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin and Germany’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Heike Peitsch. Zhumangarin congratulated the ambassador on the start of her diplomatic mission.
According to the ministry, Germany remains one of Kazakhstan’s key economic partners in Europe. Bilateral trade reached $4.5 billion last year, increasing by 13.4%. German investment in Kazakhstan has totalled $8 billion since 2005. More than 1,100 companies with German capital operate in Kazakhstan, including Knauf, CLAAS, HORSCH and Heidelberg Materials.
The two countries intend to expand existing production facilities, increase local content and involve more Kazakh suppliers in industrial cooperation. The agenda also includes boosting the production of higher value-added goods and strengthening the position of Kazakh manufacturers in the German market. A roadmap for 2026–2028 serves as the framework for these efforts.
The parties also discussed Central Asia’s role in strengthening regional connectivity and international trade. Peitsch highlighted Germany’s and other European countries’ interest in deepening cooperation with the region, noting its potential to expand trade routes and open access to new markets.
Zhumangarin emphasized the importance of developing transport links towards South Asia for Central Asia’s long-term prospects. Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify transport routes and strengthen cooperation with regional partners.
One of the projects under consideration is the construction of a railway through Afghanistan towards Pakistan. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates have already signed a memorandum of understanding on the project.
According to Peitsch, the development of such routes is of interest not only to Central Asian countries but also to Germany, as the region could become an important link between European and Asian markets. Beyond rail transport, the sides also highlighted opportunities to develop digital connectivity, gas pipelines, and oil pipelines to facilitate trade and economic cooperation.
Following the meeting, the parties agreed to continue working together on bilateral cooperation and maintain regular dialogue on key areas of Kazakhstan–Germany relations.

articles.title: Uzbekistan strengthens its relations with China and US - commonspace.eu
articles.summary: Uzbekistan strengthens its relations with China and US  commonspace.eu
articles.full_text:
In recent days, Uzbekistan welcomed the Chinese and American governments in quick succession.
During Chinese Premier Li Qiang’s visit on 17-18 October, the Uzbek presidential administration said that joint projects backed by firm agreements had reached nearly $60 billion.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio then arrived in Samarkand for C5+1 talks, accompanied at the time by American business leaders seeking contracts, particularly in critical minerals. During the visit, Uzbekistan announced 54 agreements covering trade, investment, and technology. The agreements are said to be worth a total of $12 billion, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade. However, China still accounts for 23% of Uzbekistan’s foreign trade in January-August 2026, while US goods trade with Uzbekistan totalled at $1.05 billion in 2025, which is less than a fifteenth of the value of its trade with China. Rubio said Washington was not asking Central Asian countries to stop cooperating with other partners, but would instead compete for investment.
Tashkent is likely to welcome investment from both sides, but the trade gap shows how challenging it will be if it were to decrease its dependence on Beijing.
“Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited Uzbekistan on October 17–18, just ahead of United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrived in Samarkand on October 18 with a delegation of American business leaders seeking new contracts.
While China already has a substantial presence in Uzbek manufacturing and energy, Washington is seeking to expand American involvement in critical minerals and technology. The visits highlight the growing competition between the world’s two largest economies for influence in Central Asia.
On October 17, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev received Li Qiang. According to the Uzbek presidential administration, the portfolio of joint projects backed by firm agreements has reached nearly $60 billion. More than 6,000 joint ventures with Chinese participation have been established in Uzbekistan. (...) Construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway was another topic of discussion. Work officially began in December 2024. The route will cross mountainous areas of Kyrgyzstan and connect the railway networks of China and Uzbekistan. The 304-kilometer section through Kyrgyzstan alone is estimated to cost $4.7 billion and will require 50 bridges and 29 tunnels. (...)
On October 19, Rubio attended talks in Samarkand under the C5+1 format, bringing together the U.S. and Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Rubio said nearly 300 American businesses were represented in Samarkand. Companies were discussing agreements potentially worth billions of dollars, with concrete announcements expected following the meetings. Among Washington’s priorities are critical minerals used in advanced technologies, including electronics and batteries.”
source: Caucasus and Central Asia Concise Vol 1 No 6 with Times of Central Asia
